deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivations. It is a working index or table of contents that Hilbert kept for himself. Each entry is a keyword or short thesis followed by a page reference to a notebook marked 'III' (probably one of his Notizbücher). The themes are those of his foundational and axiomatic work around 1899–1905. The previous page, on Riemann surfaces indexed by second-class ordinals, does not continue here.

Entries in order:
(1) The top line is cut off.
(2) 'Eigentlich Funktionen bilden' (forming functions proper), III p.17.
(3) 'Is there a simple theory [?]', III p.25. The key word is uncertain.
(4) If one takes as an axiom that every equation has a root, group theory (Galois theory) becomes much more harmonious. This is an algebraic-closure or adjunction-by-axiom viewpoint: the existence of roots is postulated rather than constructed.
(5) 'Similarly' III pp.107–108 and III p.108.
(6) 'Layers of axioms = rings' (Axiomenschichten = Ringe), III p.115. This is the idea of stratifying an axiom system, as in Grundlagen der Geometrie, Groups I–V.
(7) Whether a statement is provable with or without the Archimedean axiom: pp.117 and 130, corrected to 129, 'and p.131 at the very bottom', plus p.125.
(8) A crossed-out, illegible line.
(9) 'Where does mathematics begin?' III p.116.
(10) Mathematics has unconditional confidence in the solvability of its problems, III p.119. This anticipates the 1900 Paris address: 'in der Mathematik gibt es kein Ignorabimus'.
(11) The same schemata fit different disciplines, III p.119. This is the abstract, model-independent view of axiom systems.
(12) Assumptions such as 'g(x)=0 has no real root', or annulment [?]. These are hypotheses one may adjoin as axioms, as long as they are consistent.
(13) Existence of solutions of boundary-value problems [reading uncertain] equals consistency (Widerspruchslosigkeit). This is Hilbert's thesis that mathematical existence means consistency.
(14) 'Defence against Frege', III p.121. This refers to the 1899–1900 Frege–Hilbert correspondence on axioms, definitions and existence.
errors: There are no computations, so there is nothing to check mathematically.

The thesis in entry (13), that existence equals consistency, is a philosophical position, not a theorem. In full generality it is not tenable without a completeness theorem; for first-order theories, Gödel's 1930 completeness theorem justifies it after the fact.
